description: Accretion Studio is a student-led team focused on using programming, AI, data analysis, and visualization to solve real-world problems using NASA and open scientific data. We aim to turn complex datasets into practical, understandable, and innovative solutions while learning, experimenting, and building as a team.
summary: Red Frontier JAMT (Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer) is a web-based game, especially designed for ages 7-12. Within the 48-hour hackathon time frame, we developed a 3D Mars Simulation, wrote a story for the game that shows the possible future: Earth Being inhabitable for living, and 6 junior Astronauts are sent to the Mars to experiment with Resources on Mars, make clever use of resources they are Provided With, stay safe in extreme weather conditions, until they grow berries in Mars! It addresses the challenge by making junior astronaut learn and experiment about how they can optimize the use of resources on Mars to maintain their lives and also Explore a Mars simulation. It is Important as it targets a real possible future situation and teaches young minds to encounter it.
details:
The Red Frontier

The Red Frontier is a browser game where players join a six-person crew on a mission to explore Mars and build a sustainable research outpost. It opens with a short Earth-to-Mars journey, then puts players on the Martian surface to explore, scan rocks, collect supplies, operate a rover, and complete missions with different crew specialists.

Benefits and intended impact

The game teaches science through practical challenges. Players learn about Mars, geology, space weather, life support, energy, and resource planning while working together as a crew. The project aims to spark curiosity about space and STEM, and help young players build confidence in solving problems.

How it works

Players explore a 3D Martian environment in first person and can switch between six astronauts, each with a specialist role. They follow mission trails, use a scanner, manage supplies and survival systems, and build or repair equipment. NASA space-weather records and Mars map imagery add real-world context. The terrain, discoveries, and mission responses are clearly presented as game simulations where they are fictional or simplified.

Tools and technology

The project uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, and Zustand. NASA DONKI feeds and Mars Trek imagery provide selected data and map context. The game runs in a web browser and supports keyboard and touch controls. No special physical hardware is required. A small Python FastAPI backend is also included in the project.

What makes it creative

The project combines a cinematic adventure with hands-on science activities. Players learn by doing: scanning a sample, preparing for a hazard, or building a greenhouse. The crew’s distinct abilities, the mission robot B.O.L.T., and the exploration story make teamwork and discovery part of the gameplay.

Factors considered

The team designed the experience for children ages 7–12, with short objectives, clear visual guidance, science explanations, and keyboard and touch controls. It also considered teamwork, accessibility, finite supplies, browser performance, and scientific accuracy—including making clear where Mars data ends and fictional game content begins.
